thread.title: Story Stocks: Apple's "Secret" Display Manufacturing Facility Revealed, Knocking Screen Suppliers Lower (OLED)

title: Story Stocks: Apple's "Secret" Display Manufacturing Facility Revealed, Knocking Screen Suppliers Lower (OLED)
text:
Last Update: 19-Mar-18 09:52 ET Apple's "Secret" Display Manufacturing Facility Revealed, Knocking Screen Suppliers Lower (OLED) 
The cat's out of the bag, so-to-speak, regarding Apple's (AAPL) previously unknown display manufacturing facility situated near its headquarters in Cupertino, California. This is thanks to a a Bloomberg article published last night which said AAPL has been making significant strides in what it is calling MicroLED screens. For AAPL, the potential development of a game-changing screen, which could make future devices more efficient, lighter, and brighter, could represent a major catalyst as sales growth of iPhones and iPads decelerate. This covert plan came to fruition when AAPL purchased a small tech start-up called LuxVue in 2014. Back then, the acquisition didn't make many waves among investors. But, now, the implications could be massive. Over the past few years, AAPL has been investing millions into its own manufacturing facility in California. At the same time, AAPL also opened a lab in Taiwan for the purpose of testing production on a much larger scale. So far, the company has been encouraged with the results as it has given a green light for continued development over the next two years.The first AAPL product that could have the new screen is the iWatch. However, at this point, there is still plenty of uncertainty whether the new screens will make it to market. Apparently, developing MicroLED screens are far more complicated to produce than current OLED displays. The company would need to invest in all new manufacturing equipment (which could ultimately be a boon for semicap companies) and it would need to build or expand its current production facilities. Ultimately, AAPL may look to outsource production, while owning the technology outright -- which means other device OEMs may have to pay hefty royalty fees to AAPL if they use MicroLED screens.This is intriguing news for AAPL and owners of AAPL stock. It is decisively less positive for certain suppliers of OLED screens, including companies like Universal Display (OLED), LG, and Samsung, which supplies the OLED screen for AAPL's iPhone X. But, this extends beyond the actual screen, into the suppliers of components and chips for OLED screens. Specifically, a company like Synaptics (SYNA), which provides the technology to power and maneuver on OLED screens, has been a key supplier to AAPL over the years. If AAPL does ultimately make a transition to MicroLED screens, that could have a meaningful impact on its business. That said, SYNA has done well to diversify its revenue stream, so a decline in AAPL-related revenue wouldn't be quite as severe.It's also important to keep in mind, a lot can change in the matter of three plus years -- especially in the tech world. Which is the time-frame we're looking at in terms of any large-scale launch of AAPL products with new MicroLED screens. AAPL could find that it simply isn't cost-effective, and shut down the plan. Or, a different technology could emerge, making MicroLED technology not as relevant. Or, AAPL could task its current screen suppliers with developing this new technology. 
So, in conclusion, while this is certainly a major development for both AAPL and its suppliers, it is impossible to draw any real financial conclusions at this point. Consequently, investors may not want to over-react, in either direction, to today's news.
